blindSummary: The national research found no local trans statute, enforcement series or incident pattern for this state/province: its framework is entirely the national one. It is not among the 12 states/provinces that have constituted the mandated transgender welfare board, and information-access records indicate the gap stems from national-executive inaction rather than local policy. No local divergence from the national framework was documented.
blindSourceSummaries: An international human-rights organisation's statement (26 March 2026) on the national parliament's 2026 amendment to the transgender-rights law: it removes self-identification, limits recognition to the country's traditional third-gender-community and intersex categories, mandates medical certification, and creates offences carrying up to life imprisonment for 'coercing or alluring' someone to be transgender. Directly nationally-administered law in this state/province (it has no legislature of its own); no local reporting.

A national broadcaster's report (26 March 2026): both houses passed the amendment ending self-identification and mandating medical-board certification for recognition and gender-affirming surgery; protests followed, a supreme-court-appointed panel requested withdrawal, and presidential assent is pending. As a state/province without its own legislature, this unit receives the framework wholly from the centre; the piece itself has no local angle.

A national newspaper's city report (18 August 2024): a trans woman alleged a railway-security constable groped her during a 'gender check' at a metro station and made a lewd remark; authorities denied it and filed a counter-complaint. An incident from a different state/province, carried here only as a national datapoint on security screening of gender-nonconforming people in public transport spaces — a practice relevant wherever comparable checkpoints exist; no connection to this state/province.
